preceding_messages.text: I adopt the two-calendar-month, ten-reading baseline-freeze rule and the "BASELINE PENDING" comparison-cell annotation verbatim; they ensure the drift metric measures deviation from a statistically robust reference rather than from a single slush-week outlier. For the horizon-geometry question your baseline-poisoning example implies but that has remained unregulated since the installation-day sketch, I mandate a semiannual re-survey—January and July, coinciding with natural seasonal geometry shifts—where any new obstruction exceeding the archived sketch by more than five degrees in elevation angle triggers either a site-relocation review or, if relocation is impractical, a time-of-day microclimate bias term estimated from the NOAA comparison residual over the preceding four weeks and entered as a named correction line keyed to the survey date. The concrete failure this guards against: a neighbor plants a row of Japanese larches in October, bare at installation, and by July of the following year the eighteen-metre canopy shades the Stevenson screen for six afternoon hours, introducing a gradual −1.2 °C cooling bias that ramps over nine weeks, never exceeding the ±0.5 °C weekly temperature tolerance in any single week and therefore never tripping the two-week persistence gate, yet accumulating a full four-degree seasonal undercount by autumn that poisons every cross-site coherence comparison and reads to a year-two appendix auditor as a slow instrument drift that no bridging line, no serial-number change, and no post-compilation erratum can explain. I therefore require that any site whose correction-line magnitude exceeds 1.0 °C at the July survey triggers a formal relocation review identical to the three-consecutive-missing-hour rule, with the bulletin header printing "MICROCLIMATE REVIEW" alongside the affected variable's comparison cell rather than silently netting the bias into the trend.

preceding_messages.speaker: Y
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the semiannual re-survey cadence, the five-degree obstruction threshold, the NOAA-residual bias-term estimation, and the 1.0 °C relocation-review trigger verbatim; they convert the larch-canopy failure from a nine-week invisible ramp into a flagged, correctable, auditable entry. The four-week residual regression your correction line depends on, however, is itself vulnerable to contamination: if the NOAA comparison station underwent a site migration, instrument replacement, or published a quality-control exclusion during those four weeks, the residual conflates the neighbour's shade bias with the comparison station's own discontinuity and attributes the latter to the microclimate term, netting in a correction that compensates the wrong artifact. I therefore mandate that before any correction line is executed the compiler must verify, from the NOAA station's published metadata record, that no site-migration flag, instrument-replacement entry, or quality-control exclusion falls inside the four-week estimation window; if any such flag is present the correction line is deferred and the affected comparison cells print "NOAA DISCONTINUITY — CORRECTION DEFERRED" rather than a populated bias term, so a year-two appendix auditor never mistakes a comparison-station artifact for a neighbourhood-scale microclimate shift.

target.speaker: X
target.text: I adopt the NOAA-metadata verification gate and the "NOAA DISCONTINUITY — CORRECTION DEFERRED" annotation verbatim. Because that gate catches only formally logged events, I further mandate a sliding-window coherence check on the NOAA comparison column itself: any rolling eight-week cumulative drift exceeding ±0.4 °C—roughly the signature of an unflagged 0.05 °C/week thermistor creep—invalidates the four-week estimation window and defers the correction line under the same annotation. The failure this closes is that the NOAA station four kilometres east accumulates a silent +0.1 °C/week thermistor drift over six weeks with no replacement entry in its metadata, the compiler's weeks 3–6 window absorbs +0.4 °C of that drift, freezes a spurious +1.0 °C microclimate bias term into the neighborhood site, and suppresses every subsequent comparison cell by that amount, so that a genuine October larch-canopy-closure cooling of 1.2 °C reads as only −0.2 °C and vanishes below the ±0.5 °C weekly tolerance. Any week in which the eight-week coherence check trips therefore prints "NOAA DRIFT — CORRECTION DEFERRED" in the affected comparison cell, with the deferred correction queued for re-estimation once a clean four-week window resumes.
